knowledge_point.title: Integrating a Product of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities

question.:question/worked-solution:
We multiply out the parentheses and then use the identity $\tan(x)=\frac{\sin(x)}{\cos(x)},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \tan(x)(\sec(x)+5\,\cos(x))\,\text{d}x &=\int (\tan(x)\sec(x)+5\,\tan(x)\cdot \cos(x))\,\text{d}x \\ &=\int (\sec(x)\tan(x)+5\,\frac{\sin(x)}{\cos(x)}\cdot \cos(x))\,\text{d}x \\ &=\int (\sec(x)\tan(x)+5\,\sin(x))\,\text{d}x \\ &=\int \sec(x)\tan(x)\,\text{d}x+5\,\int \sin(x)\,\text{d}x \\ &=- 5 \cos{\left(x \right)} + \sec{\left(x \right)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating a Product of Trigonometric Functions Using Trigonometric Identities

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the identity $\tan(5 x)=\frac{\sin(5 x)}{\cos(5 x)}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{30}} \cos(5 x)\tan(5 x)\,\text{d}x &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{30}} \cos(5 x)\cdot \frac{\sin(5 x)}{\cos(5 x)}\,\text{d}x \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{30}} \sin(5 x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=5 x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=5 x.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{30}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{6}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{30}} \sin(5 x)\,\text{d}x &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \sin(u)\cdot \frac{1}{5}\,\text{d}u \\ &=\frac{1}{5}\,\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \sin(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &=- \frac{\cos{\left(u \right)}}{5}\big|_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &=- \frac{1}{5}\,(\cos(\frac{\pi}{6})-\cos(0)) \\ &=- \frac{1}{5}\,(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1) \\ &=\frac{1}{5} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{10}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the identity $\sec(x)=\frac{1}{\cos(x)}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{- \frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{12}} 5\,\sec(2 x)\cos^{2}(2 x)\,\text{d}x &=5\,\int_{- \frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{12}} \frac{1}{\cos(2 x)}\cdot \cos^{2}(2 x)\,\text{d}x \\ &=5\,\int_{- \frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{12}} \cos(2 x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this by substitution. Let $u=2 x.$ Then $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.$

Now, we fill the table for the limits of integration, according to the rule $u=2 x.$

| $x$ | $- \frac{\pi}{6}$ | $\frac{\pi}{12}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $- \frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{\pi}{6}$ |

Therefore, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\begin{aligned}5\,\int_{- \frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{12}} \cos(2 x)\,\text{d}x &=5\,\int_{- \frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \cos(u)\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\ &=\frac{5}{2}\,\int_{- \frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \cos(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &=\frac{5 \sin{\left(u \right)}}{2}\big|_{- \frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &=\frac{5}{2}\,(\sin(\frac{\pi}{6})-\sin(- \frac{\pi}{3})) \\ &=\frac{5}{2}\,(\frac{1}{2}-- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ &=\frac{5}{4} + \frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$
